text: By ending your membership you will lose access to your Prime benefits.
rationale: Explicit loss framing in the cancellation flow. Emphasizes what user will lose rather than neutral confirmation. Designed to trigger loss aversion and discourage cancellation.
risk_outcome: User abandons cancellation due to fear of losing benefits

text: Paige, do you still want to end your Prime for Young Adults benefits?
rationale: Personalized guilt-tripping using first name. Reframes cancellation as 'ending benefits' rather than 'stopping charges'. Creates emotional friction.
risk_outcome: User feels personally addressed and guilty about canceling

text: You still have 13 days left to enjoy your Prime for Young Adults benefits until the next billing cycle
rationale: Reminds user of remaining paid time to create sunk cost feeling. Implies waste if they cancel now. Borderline - could be seen as helpful info.
risk_outcome: User delays cancellation and forgets, gets charged again

text: By cancelling, you will lose access to 5% back on eligible purchases with your Prime Visa. You've earned $87.70 from 5% back over the last 12 statements, and you will keep your already-earned rewards.
rationale: Classic sunk cost manipulation. Shows specific dollar amount ($87.70) user has 'earned' to make cancellation feel like throwing away money. The earned value anchor makes continuing feel like protecting an investment.
risk_outcome: User keeps subscription to avoid 'losing' the cashback benefit

text: By cancelling, you will no longer be eligible for your unclaimed Prime exclusive offers.
rationale: Vague threat about losing 'unclaimed offers' without specifying what they are. Creates FOMO about unknown future value. User can't evaluate what they're actually losing.
risk_outcome: User worries about missing unknown valuable offers

text: If you cancel, you will immediately lose your remaining words: 16,768
rationale: Explicit threat of immediate loss of paid credits. Uses specific number (16,768) to make loss feel concrete and painful. Red warning icon and text color amplify urgency. Classic sunk cost manipulation.
risk_outcome: User abandons cancellation to avoid losing credits they already paid for

text: Are you sure you want to cancel? We have new updates every week that keep you at the forefront of AI tech.
rationale: Creates FOMO about vague future features. No specific dates or concrete features promised. Implies user will fall behind competitors if they cancel. Roadmap shown without timelines.
risk_outcome: User stays subscribed waiting for features that may never arrive

text: Opt for a subscription pause instead of canceling, and unlock a bonus of 10,000 free word credits the moment you return!
rationale: Incentivizes pause over cancel. Pause keeps user in billing system and easier to resume charges. The 'bonus' creates obligation to return. Framed as benefit but maintains subscription relationship.
risk_outcome: User pauses instead of cancels, forgets, and gets charged when pause ends

text: Get FREE Two-Day Shipping
rationale: FTC cited this as Interface Interference. Prominent button emphasized 'FREE' shipping while hiding that clicking enrolls user in $14.99/month auto-renewing Prime subscription. Option to decline was comparatively inconspicuous link.
risk_outcome: User unknowingly enrolls in $139/year subscription thinking they are just getting free shipping on one order
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: No thanks, I don't want FREE Two-Day Shipping
rationale: FTC cited as Confirmshaming. Decline option used emotive language to guilt users. Framing declining Prime as rejecting 'FREE' shipping rather than declining paid subscription. Settlement specifically banned this language.
risk_outcome: User feels foolish declining 'free' benefit, enrolls in subscription they don't want
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Start your 30-day free trial
rationale: FTC alleged Amazon engaged in Sneaking by hiding or delaying disclosure of Prime's price and auto-renewal feature. Material terms like $14.99/month charge after trial buried in small font while 'free trial' emphasized.
risk_outcome: User enrolls in trial without understanding auto-renewal at $14.99/month
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Are you sure? You'll lose FREE Two-Day Shipping on millions of items
rationale: Part of Amazon's 'Iliad Flow' cancellation process. FTC cited this as Obstruction/Roach Motel technique. Multiple pages of loss-framing designed to thwart cancellation. Required 4-page, 6-click, 15-option flow to cancel.
risk_outcome: User abandons cancellation due to fear of losing benefits
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Keep my benefits
rationale: Prominent button in cancellation flow. FTC cited asymmetric presentation - 'Keep benefits' button prominent while cancel option less visible. Part of Iliad Flow obstruction pattern.
risk_outcome: User clicks prominent button to stop annoying flow, accidentally keeps subscription
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Remind me later
rationale: Diversionary option in cancellation flow. FTC cited multiple diversions including discount offers, benefit reminders, and delay options designed to prevent completion of cancellation.
risk_outcome: User postpones cancellation, forgets, gets charged again
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: You'll lose access to Prime Video, including thousands of movies and TV shows
rationale: Loss framing in cancellation flow. Part of 15-option obstruction flow. Emphasizes loss of streaming content to discourage cancellation.
risk_outcome: User abandons cancellation to keep video access
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Easy Cancellation – If your family does not love ABCmouse, you can cancel at any time!
rationale: FTC found this claim deceptive. Despite promising 'Easy Cancellation', actual cancellation required navigating confusing multi-page process with promotions designed to prevent completion. Hundreds of thousands of consumers who visited cancellation path remained subscribed.
risk_outcome: User signs up believing cancellation is easy when it is actually designed to be difficult
case_citation: FTC v. Age of Learning Inc., No. 2:20-cv-7996 (C.D. Cal. 2020)

text: Special Offer: 12 months for $59.95
rationale: FTC alleged this failed to disclose that subscription would automatically renew indefinitely at full price. No clear disclosure that $59.95 charge would repeat annually without action. Relied on hyperlinked terms and conditions for disclosure.
risk_outcome: User charged $59.95 annually without realizing subscription auto-renews
case_citation: FTC v. Age of Learning Inc., No. 2:20-cv-7996 (C.D. Cal. 2020)

text: Continue your learning journey - Extend your membership now!
rationale: FTC cited cluttered cancellation pages with advertisements and promotions aimed at convincing consumer not to cancel. If consumer clicked any promotional link, cancellation process stopped and they had to start over.
risk_outcome: User accidentally clicks promotion, loses progress in cancellation flow
case_citation: FTC v. Age of Learning Inc., No. 2:20-cv-7996 (C.D. Cal. 2020)

text: Your child has earned 847 tickets and unlocked 23 prizes! Keep their progress going.
rationale: Sunk cost manipulation targeting parents through children's achievements. FTC noted cancellation path included multiple pages of promotional content designed to prevent cancellation completion.
risk_outcome: Parent abandons cancellation to preserve child's virtual rewards
case_citation: FTC v. Age of Learning Inc., No. 2:20-cv-7996 (C.D. Cal. 2020)

text: To cancel your service, please call our retention team at [phone number]
rationale: FTC found Vonage allowed easy online signup but forced phone-only cancellation starting 2017. Phone number was obscured on website, hours limited, and calls frequently dropped. Internal email said customers were 'sent in a circle when they want to downgrade or remove the service.'
risk_outcome: User cannot cancel online despite signing up online, must navigate phone maze
case_citation: FTC v. Vonage Holdings Corp., No. 3:22-cv-06435 (D.N.J. 2022)

text: Before you go, let me tell you about some great offers that could save you money
rationale: FTC cited lengthy sales pitches during cancellation calls. Retention agents were given monetary incentives to prevent cancellations. Customers endured repeated pitches before being allowed to cancel.
risk_outcome: User gives up on cancellation due to exhausting phone process
case_citation: FTC v. Vonage Holdings Corp., No. 3:22-cv-06435 (D.N.J. 2022)

text: Your early termination fee will be $[amount]
rationale: FTC found early termination fees were not clearly disclosed at signup but surprised customers during cancellation. Sometimes totaled hundreds of dollars. Constituted 'junk fees' designed to deter cancellation.
risk_outcome: User keeps unwanted service to avoid unexpected fee
case_citation: FTC v. Vonage Holdings Corp., No. 3:22-cv-06435 (D.N.J. 2022)

text: Your cancellation request has been processed
rationale: FTC found Vonage continued charging customers AFTER they received cancellation confirmation. When customers complained, they received only partial refunds. This constituted unauthorized billing.
risk_outcome: User believes service is cancelled but continues to be charged
case_citation: FTC v. Vonage Holdings Corp., No. 3:22-cv-06435 (D.N.J. 2022)

text: Order Now to Enter!
rationale: FTC found Publishers Clearing House used dark patterns to mislead consumers about how to enter sweepstakes. Made consumers believe purchase was necessary to enter when free entry was available but obscured.
risk_outcome: User makes unnecessary purchase believing it is required for sweepstakes entry
case_citation: FTC v. Publishers Clearing House LLC (2023)

text: Your entry has been processed. Complete your order to finalize.
rationale: FTC alleged PCH made it appear purchase completion was necessary for sweepstakes entry. $18.5M settlement for deceptive negative option marketing.
risk_outcome: User completes purchase thinking it finalizes sweepstakes entry
case_citation: FTC v. Publishers Clearing House LLC (2023)

text: Limited Time Offer - Enroll Now Before Rates Increase!
rationale: FTC cited false urgency in health insurance marketing. $100M settlement for deceptive practices including fake limited-time offers. Rates were not actually increasing.
risk_outcome: User enrolls hastily in unsuitable insurance plan due to fake deadline
case_citation: FTC v. Benefytt Technologies Inc. (2022)

text: Only 3 spots remaining at this price!
rationale: FTC found Benefytt used fabricated scarcity claims to pressure enrollment. Part of $100M settlement for deceptive enrollment practices.
risk_outcome: User enrolls without proper comparison shopping due to fake scarcity
case_citation: FTC v. Benefytt Technologies Inc. (2022)

text: You're Pre-Approved!
rationale: FTC found Credit Karma deceived consumers with false pre-approval claims. Users were told they were pre-approved but then rejected after providing personal information. $3M settlement.
risk_outcome: User shares personal/financial data expecting approval that doesn't exist
case_citation: FTC v. Credit Karma LLC (2022)

text: 90% approval odds - Apply now!
rationale: FTC internal A/B testing showed 'Excellent odds' language increased clicks. Company chose deceptive claim despite knowing users were rejected at much higher rates.
risk_outcome: User applies expecting approval, damages credit score with rejection
case_citation: FTC v. Credit Karma LLC (2022)

text: No thanks, I don't want to save money
rationale: Classic confirmshaming pattern documented on deceptive.design. Decline option forces user to self-identify as someone who dislikes saving money. Creates social identity threat to deter opting out of marketing emails.
risk_outcome: User signs up for unwanted marketing emails to avoid self-shaming

text: No, I prefer to pay full price
rationale: Confirmshaming pattern from deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Opt-out is framed as an irrational financial choice. Forces user to affirm they prefer paying more, creating cognitive dissonance that drives sign-up.
risk_outcome: User provides email to avoid feeling foolish about declining discount

text: No, I don't want to stay alive
rationale: Extreme confirmshaming from MyMedic.com (2018) documented in deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Opt-out label equates declining a newsletter with choosing death. Exploits mortality fear for email capture. Particularly harmful given target audience of first responders.
risk_outcome: User surrenders email under extreme emotional duress from death-framing

text: I don't read.
rationale: Confirmshaming from Esquire documented on deceptive.design. Declining the newsletter is framed as illiteracy. Weaponizes intellectual identity to guilt users into subscribing.
risk_outcome: User subscribes to avoid being labeled as someone who does not read

text: No, I REALLY hate saving money
rationale: Intensified confirmshaming documented on deceptive.design. Capitalized emphasis on 'REALLY' doubles down on shaming. User must not only decline but emphatically affirm an irrational preference.
risk_outcome: User submits email to avoid affirming exaggerated irrational identity

text: Hurry up! Sale ending in 11 Hrs, 59 Mins, 46 Sec. Sale Ends Once The Timer Hits Zero!
rationale: Fake countdown timer from Shopify 'Hurrify' app documented on deceptive.design. Timer is configured to loop infinitely when it reaches zero (evergreen mode). The urgency is entirely fabricated.
risk_outcome: User makes impulse purchase under false time pressure that does not actually exist

text: Limited time only
rationale: Fake limited-time message from Samsung documented on deceptive.design. The offer ran continuously for months (Nov-Dec 2022) and actually increased in value. No real deadline existed despite 'limited time' framing.
risk_outcome: User rushes purchase believing deal will expire when it is perpetually available

text: Only 2 rooms left at this price!
rationale: Fake scarcity message commonly seen on booking platforms, documented on deceptive.design. Stock numbers are often fabricated or algorithmically generated on each page load, not reflecting real inventory.
risk_outcome: User books immediately without comparison shopping due to fabricated scarcity

text: 3 other people are looking at this right now
rationale: Fake social proof / activity message documented on deceptive.design. Creates artificial competitive pressure by claiming others are viewing the same item. Numbers are often randomly generated or grossly inflated.
risk_outcome: User rushes to purchase fearing someone else will buy the item first

text: Sale ends soon
rationale: Vague urgency message from Chicwish documented in Princeton/Chicago deceptive patterns study cited on deceptive.design. No end date specified, withholding information to create open-ended anxiety. Sale remains active indefinitely.
risk_outcome: User purchases hastily under vague deadline that never materializes

text: Only 1 left in stock — order soon
rationale: Fake low-stock warning documented on deceptive.design. Amazon and similar platforms show persistent low-stock labels that do not reflect actual inventory. Princeton study found some sites randomly generated stock numbers on each page load.
risk_outcome: User makes impulse purchase to avoid missing out on falsely scarce item

text: Lightning Deal — Limited Time Offer!
rationale: Amazon Lightning Deal urgency pattern documented on deceptive.design. Countdown timers and scarcity labels create artificial pressure. Actual availability often far exceeds what is implied by the urgency framing.
risk_outcome: User skips comparison shopping and purchases impulsively under fabricated deadline

text: To cancel your subscription, please contact our support team
rationale: Hard-to-cancel pattern from the New York Times documented on deceptive.design. Despite easy online subscription, cancellation requires contacting support. Chat agents use scripted retention pitches. Creates asymmetric friction — the roach motel pattern.
risk_outcome: User gives up on cancellation due to friction and continues paying

text: To cancel, please call our retention team
rationale: Phone-only cancellation from Savage X Fenty documented on deceptive.design. The $49.95/month membership can only be cancelled by calling customer support, while sign-up is fully online. Classic roach motel asymmetry.
risk_outcome: User continues paying subscription because phone cancellation is too burdensome

text: Are you sure you want to leave? Your friends will miss you!
rationale: Emotional guilt trip in cancellation flows documented on deceptive.design. Combines hard-to-cancel obstruction with confirmshaming. Frames leaving as social abandonment to trigger loss aversion around relationships.
risk_outcome: User abandons account deletion to avoid perceived social loss

text: Service Fee: $24.50
rationale: Hidden costs pattern from Ticketmaster documented on deceptive.design. Base ticket price shown prominently; service fees, processing fees, and delivery fees only revealed at final checkout. By that point user has invested time selecting seats and entering details.
risk_outcome: User pays significantly more than advertised price due to drip pricing

text: Processing Fee: $8.95 | Facility Charge: $3.50 | Order Processing Fee: $5.00
rationale: Multiple hidden fees stacked at checkout, documented on deceptive.design. Each fee is individually small but collectively substantial. Splitting into many fees also makes comparison shopping impossible — a form of Comparison Prevention.
risk_outcome: User pays 30-40% more than expected due to stacked hidden fees

text: Sports Direct Mug + Magazine — £1.00
rationale: Sneak into basket from Sports Direct documented on deceptive.design and BBC Watchdog. Unwanted mug and magazine automatically added to cart without user consent. User must actively spot and remove the item, which is easily overlooked.
risk_outcome: User unknowingly pays for unrequested item bundled into cart

text: Added for your protection: 1 Year Security Software
rationale: Sneak into basket from Laptop Outlet documented on deceptive.design. Security software and mouse auto-added when purchasing laptop. 'Added for your protection' frames unwanted addition as a safety measure, exploiting authority claim.
risk_outcome: User pays for unwanted software and accessories auto-added to cart

text: Start your free trial — credit card required
rationale: Forced continuity pattern documented on deceptive.design. Credit card is collected for a 'free' trial with auto-renewal buried in terms. Exploits Status Quo bias — users who forget to cancel are automatically charged, as documented on Netflix and Hulu.
risk_outcome: User is auto-charged after forgetting to cancel before trial ends

text: $0 today, then $14.99/month
rationale: Forced continuity documented on deceptive.design. '$0 today' dominates visual hierarchy while recurring charge is de-emphasized. Anchors user on zero cost while obscuring ongoing financial commitment.
risk_outcome: User signs up perceiving zero cost, gets locked into monthly charges

text: Create an account to continue reading
rationale: Forced action pattern documented on deceptive.design. User wants to read content but is forced to create an account first, surrendering personal data. The account creation often includes hidden marketing consent and data sharing agreements.
risk_outcome: User shares personal data unnecessarily to access content

text: Use our app for the best experience
rationale: Nagging pattern from Reddit documented on deceptive.design. Persistent prompts push users to download the app despite clear disinterest. Implies inferior experience if they continue on web, creating mild fear of missing out.
risk_outcome: User downloads app granting broader device permissions than web browsing requires

text: We've alerted you multiple times that this printer had non-Original HP cartridges installed. This is your final notice to fix the issue.
rationale: Aggressive nagging from HP documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Frames third-party cartridge use as a 'problem' user must 'fix'. Escalating threat language (multiple alerts, final notice) pressures purchase of expensive OEM cartridges.
risk_outcome: User buys overpriced OEM cartridges due to intimidating printer DRM messaging

text: Use this activity
rationale: Privacy zuckering from Facebook documented on deceptive.design. 'Use this activity' obscures that user is consenting to data collection and targeted advertising. Deliberately vague label avoids stating what the user is actually agreeing to.
risk_outcome: User consents to broad data collection without understanding the scope

text: Make Microsoft Edge your default browser for the best experience on Windows
rationale: Nagging pattern from Microsoft documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Pop-ups appear during full-screen activities (e.g., gaming) to push Edge. Implies degraded experience unless user complies. Uses OS-level authority to pressure browser choice.
risk_outcome: User switches browser defaults due to persistent interruption, not informed choice

text: Annual plan, paid monthly
rationale: Hidden subscription commitment from Adobe documented on deceptive.design and DOJ lawsuit. 'Annual plan, paid monthly' obscures that user is locked into 12-month commitment. Early termination fee buried in fine print and optional text boxes.
risk_outcome: User believes they have a monthly plan but faces early termination fees

text: Sarah from New York just bought this item 2 minutes ago
rationale: Fake social proof activity notification documented on deceptive.design. Fabricated purchase notifications with fake names and locations create illusion of high demand. 87% of consumers report seeing these messages, per OECD survey.
risk_outcome: User purchases impulsively believing product is in high demand when activity is fabricated

text: Upgrade to Premium for the best experience
rationale: Comparison prevention documented on deceptive.design. Vague 'best experience' language avoids specifying what Premium includes that free/basic does not. Makes rational comparison impossible, pushing emotional decision-making.
risk_outcome: User upgrades to more expensive tier without understanding the actual differences

text: Share — Can edit
rationale: Sneaking pattern from Figma documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Share button with 'Can edit' silently adds billable seats. Unlike Google Docs, sharing triggers per-seat charges. Corporate credit card holders often do not notice the incremental costs.
risk_outcome: Organization incurs unexpected seat charges from routine sharing actions

text: I would like to receive updates through the newsletter
rationale: Pre-selection dark pattern documented on deceptive.design. Checkbox is pre-selected by default so user is automatically opted into marketing emails. Users who do not notice or do not uncheck consent without informed decision.
risk_outcome: User unknowingly opts into marketing communications via pre-checked consent

text: Uncheck this box if you prefer not to not receive promotional emails
rationale: Trick question pattern documented on deceptive.design. Double negative ('prefer not to not receive') confuses user intent. Processing the sentence requires cognitive effort that most users will not invest during fast form completion.
risk_outcome: User makes unintended consent choice due to deliberately confusing language

text: Accept cookies to continue viewing this content
rationale: Cookie wall from HRAcuity documented on deceptive.design. Forces cookie acceptance to view a YouTube embed that does not require cookies. Forced action pattern — user must consent to tracking to access otherwise freely available content.
risk_outcome: User consents to unnecessary tracking to access content available without cookies

text: Your subscription has been automatically upgraded to the $99.99/year plan
rationale: Bait and switch from Microsoft documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Users were silently upgraded to a more expensive subscription tier. Downgrading back required going through the full cancellation flow to find the original pricing option.
risk_outcome: User pays 43% more annually without consenting to the upgrade

text: Download
rationale: Disguised ad pattern documented on deceptive.design. Fake 'Download' button styled to look like the actual download CTA on software download sites. Clicking leads to ad/malware instead of intended file. Exploits UI familiarity and urgency.
risk_outcome: User installs unwanted software or malware believing they clicked legitimate download

text: Find friends already on the platform — import your contacts
rationale: Friend spam pattern from LinkedIn documented on deceptive.design. Contact import is framed as finding friends but actually sends mass invitations to entire address book. LinkedIn paid $13M in settlement over this practice.
risk_outcome: User's entire contact list receives spam invitations without informed consent

text: Your content may be used to improve Figma AI features
rationale: Sneaking/forced action from Figma (early 2025) documented on deceptive.design. All users were automatically opted in to having design files used for AI training. Opt-out required finding and toggling a buried setting. Similar to Meta AI training opt-out controversy.
risk_outcome: Proprietary design files are used for AI training without meaningful user consent

text: 450 Robux for $4.99
rationale: Virtual currency obfuscation targeting children documented on deceptive.design. Converting real money to virtual currency (Robux) disconnects spending from financial reality. Children described the conversion as 'scary' and confusing, leading to unintentional overspending.
risk_outcome: Children overspend real money through confusing virtual currency conversion

text: Subscribe to Premium for push notifications when baby wakes — $9.99/month
rationale: Feature paywall after purchase documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Previously free push notifications locked behind $9.99/month subscription after a hardware purchase ($400). Exploits sunk cost and parental concern to coerce ongoing payments.
risk_outcome: Parent pays recurring subscription to access feature that was free at time of hardware purchase

text: You have a pre-approved personal loan! Get started
rationale: Pre-approved loan trick documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. 'Get started' button has a pre-checked consent checkbox above it for credit score checking. User clicks the inviting CTA without noticing they are consenting to a hard credit inquiry.
risk_outcome: User triggers hard credit inquiry thinking they are just viewing loan details
